title: The gamma function
summary: $\Gamma(s) = \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx$ extends the factorial, $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$, to a meromorphic function with poles at $0, -1, -2, \dots$. Euler introduced it in 1729.
why: It is the factor that makes the zeta function's functional equation symmetric.

leads_to.title: The Mellin transform and Perron's formula

timeline.title: The gamma function
timeline.text: Interpolated $n!$ to non-integers in letters to Goldbach.

title: Fourier analysis and Poisson summation
summary: Poisson summation says $\sum_n f(n) = \sum_n \hat f(n)$. Since $e^{-\pi x^2}$ is its own Fourier transform, the theta function $\theta(t) = \sum_n e^{-\pi n^2 t}$ satisfies $\theta(1/t) = \sqrt t\,\theta(t)$; Riemann built the functional equation from this.
why: Duality between a function and its transform reappears in the large sieve and the circle method.

timeline.title: Théorie analytique de la chaleur
timeline.text: Expanded functions in trigonometric series to solve the heat equation.

title: The Mellin transform and Perron's formula
summary: The Mellin transform $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,x^{s-1}\,dx$ moves between functions of $x$ and Dirichlet-series-like functions of $s$. Perron's formula recovers partial sums $\sum_{n \le x} a_n$ from $\sum a_n n^{-s}$ by a contour integral.
why: The 2026 quasi-RH manuscript lists a Mellin continuation as a key step.
references: Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory
Montgomery & Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I

timeline.title: Quasi-RH manuscript (7/8)
timeline.text: Claims every Dirichlet $L$-function is zero-free in $\operatorname{Re}s > \tfrac78$, using Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, cubic theta sums and a Mellin continuation. Reported as Lean-verified.

title: Dirichlet series and Euler products
summary: Series $\sum a_n n^{-s}$. When $a_n$ is multiplicative the series factors over primes; for $a_n = 1$ this is Euler's 1737 product, an analytic restatement of unique factorization.
why: The product shows $\sum 1/p$ diverges and ties primes to the poles and zeros of a function.
references: Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory

prerequisites.title: Primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic

leads_to.title: Dirichlet L-functions and primes in progressions

timeline.title: The Euler product
timeline.text: $\sum n^{-s} = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$, and with it the divergence of $\sum 1/p$.

title: The Riemann zeta function
summary: $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$ for $\operatorname{Re}s > 1$ continues to all of $\mathbb C$ except a simple pole at $s = 1$. Euler found $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ in 1735; Riemann's 1859 paper made $\zeta$ a function of a complex variable.
references: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function

leads_to.title: Dirichlet L-functions and primes in progressions

timeline.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
timeline.text: Continued $\zeta$ to the complex plane, proved the functional equation, linked zeros to primes and stated the Riemann hypothesis.

title: Functional equation and trivial zeros
summary: The completed function $\xi(s) = \tfrac12 s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ satisfies $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$. So nontrivial zeros are symmetric about $\operatorname{Re}s = \tfrac12$, and $\zeta$ has trivial zeros at $-2, -4, -6, \dots$.
why: Symmetry means any zero-free region near $\operatorname{Re}s=1$ gives one near $\operatorname{Re}s=0$.
references: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function

prerequisites.title: The Mellin transform and Perron's formula

leads_to.title: Nontrivial zeros and the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula

timeline.title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
timeline.text: Continued $\zeta$ to the complex plane, proved the functional equation, linked zeros to primes and stated the Riemann hypothesis.

title: Chebyshev and von Mangoldt functions
summary: $\Lambda(n) = \log p$ if $n = p^k$ and $0$ otherwise; $\psi(x) = \sum_{n \le x} \Lambda(n)$ counts primes with weight $\log p$. Chebyshev (1848–1850) showed $\psi(x) \asymp x$.
why: $\psi$ is the natural prime-counting function for analysis: the prime number theorem is $\psi(x) \sim x$.
references: Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory

timeline.title: Chebyshev's estimates
timeline.text: Showed $\pi(x)\log x / x$ stays between two constants.

timeline.title: Proof of the explicit formula
timeline.text: Proved Riemann's formula for $\psi(x)$ as a sum over zeros.
